title: Dragons' Den IP Blog - Series 23 Episode 13

content.content: Another nail-biting episode of Dragons' Den tonight, featuring pawfect personalised pet paraphernalia and queue-busting entrepreneurs, hoping to win over the Dragons.
A dog-gone success
First through the doors of either doom or delight was Lucy Bowes and her pretty pooch, Lola.

Lola's adorable little growl at something off-stage briefly distracted me, but I was back in the room as Lucy introduced Lucy & Lola, a business creating hand-drawn pet portraits embroidered onto clothing and accessories.

As a pet owner myself, I found it hard not to imagine my three cats stitched onto a cosy sweatshirt in time for winter. The Dragons didn't have to imagine though - Lucy arrived bearing gifts, presenting them each with a sweatshirt featuring their own beloved pet, leaving Jenna Meek a little misty eyed (and me a little jealous).
A quick peak at the IPO trade mark register shows Lucy has taken steps to protect the Lucy & Lola brand, securing a registered UK trade mark for her brand name.

Seeking £100k for 10% of the business, Lucy explained how the idea came shortly after adopting Lola in 2021. What started as a way to show off one very cute dog grew into a thriving business, attracting more than 45,000 customers and generating more than £3 million in revenue since its launch.

After hearing the numbers, the Dragons seemed keen to get their claws into the company. Peter Jones was first to bite, offering the full £100,000 for 20%. Deborah Meaden and Touker Suleyman followed with matching offers. Steven Bartlett and Jenna initially suggested mentorship might be more valuable than investment, but after Lucy explained she wanted both, Jenna joined the growing list of interested Dragons, prompting a U-turn from Steven.
Jenna agreed to his suggestion of a joint offer and Lucy, after some negotiating, got them to agree to reduce their combined stake to 15% once they had recouped their investment.
Pretty impressive for a business born from a pencil and a pooch.
Flushed with success
Next through the doors were Amber Probyn and Hazel McShane, co-founders of Peequal and creators of a product that immediately had me thinking, “where was this in my festival-going heyday?!”

Designed with festivals in mind, Peequal is a flat-pack, squat-and-go women's urinal, intended to tackle one of festival life's longest-standing frustrations - lengthy toilet queues. I still have flashbacks of being stuck in the world’s worst toilet queue at Glastonbury as my favourite band belted out my favourite song, gutted I was where I was and not two feet deep in the crowd.
According to their research, Peequal is significantly quicker to use than a traditional temporary toilet and its portable, waterless design reduces transport and environmental impacts.

Seeking £100k for 2% of the company, Amber and Hazel brought a working demonstration into the Den. Jenna was more game for a mock test of the product than Deborah, although eventually even Touker gave it a try.
Questions quickly turned to how the business was protected, and my ears pricked up as quickly as Lola's earlier in the episode.

Amber and Hazel showed the Dragons they were IP savvy, explaining that Peequal is protected by a registered design (GB6189902) as well as a granted patent (GB2606016) in the UK. The business also has patent applications pending overseas.

In fact, a quick bit of detective work revealed a hat trick of intellectual property (IP) rights. Alongside designs and patents, Amber and Hazel have protected the Peequal brand and logo with trade marks.
Designs versus patents – which is best for you?

The Peequal is a great example of how different IP rights can work to protect a growing business. Registered designs are one of the quickest and cheapest ways to protect a product's appearance, while patents are more complex, cost more and take longer to secure. We would always recommend seeking advice from an IP attorney before deciding which route is right for you.

Careful planning matters too. If a design is published before a patent application is filed, that disclosure may become 'prior art'. As a result, features of the invention may no longer be considered new, potentially affecting the validity of a later patent application.

You may also have noticed that overseas protection was mentioned in the episode. IP rights are territorial, meaning protection only applies in the countries where it has been granted or registered. Fortunately, international agreements exist to make it easier for businesses to extend their protection beyond the UK. Find out more about protecting your IP abroad on our website.

title: Mucky Nutz receives a King’s Award for Enterprise in Innovation

content.content: We are proud to share that Mucky Nutz holds the 2026 King’s Award for Enterprise, Innovation for our Rear MugGuard.

The King’s Awards for Enterprise are among the UK’s most prestigious business awards. Approved personally by His Majesty The King, they celebrate outstanding achievement by UK businesses and mark 60 years of recognising excellence.

Based in Bude, Cornwall, Mucky Nutz is an independent cycling accessories brand with a team of just four people. Receiving this recognition is an especially proud moment for us and shows what can be achieved through persistence, practical problem-solving and listening closely to customers.
What the Award recognises
The Award recognises the innovation behind our Rear MugGuard: a modular and adjustable rear mudguard designed specifically for modern mountain bikes.

Traditional rear mudguards often force riders to choose between a small guard that protects the bike’s rear shock and linkage, or a larger guard that provides fuller protection for the rider. The Rear MugGuard was created to offer both options in one adaptable product.

It can be used in a shorter configuration for everyday protection or fitted with its extension for greater coverage in wet and muddy conditions. Riders can switch between the two without tools, while an adjustment dial allows the angle and clearance to be fine-tuned for different bikes.

The Rear MugGuard was conceived and developed in the UK and is manufactured here from 100% recycled plastic. It is supplied in a reusable kit bag made from recycled bottles, avoiding the need for single-use packaging. The product was developed over several years through research, prototyping and extensive real-world testing. It has since become one of the most important products in the Mucky Nutz range.
Why it matters to the business
The Award is a powerful recognition of what can be achieved through careful product development, determination and listening closely to customers.
It also reflects the support of our UK manufacturing partners, distributors, retailers and riders around the world.
Developing the Rear MugGuard strengthened our experience and capabilities in design, prototyping, testing and manufacturing, giving us greater confidence to take on more ambitious projects.

It also provides an opportunity to reflect on how far the business has come. What began with a simple mudguard idea has grown into a recognised British cycling brand, designing products in Cornwall and selling them to riders around the world. Recipients are entitled to use the King’s Awards Emblem for five years, in line with official guidance, and will receive the Award locally from His Majesty’s Lord-Lieutenant.
Shane Darwin, Founder and Managing Director, Mucky Nutz, said:
Top tips for future applicants
We would encourage other small businesses not to be put off by the application process or assume that the Awards are only for larger organisations.

Allow plenty of time, gather your evidence early and explain your achievement clearly. Do not assume the assessors already understand your industry or product. Describe the problem you identified, what you did differently and the measurable difference it has made.
It is also worth being honest about the challenges involved. Innovation rarely follows a straight line, and the setbacks, changes and lessons learned are an important part of the story.

Most importantly, do not underestimate what a small team can achieve. A business does not need enormous resources to create something genuinely innovative. It needs a strong idea, evidence that it works and the persistence to keep improving it.
Find out more..
Find out more about Mucky Nutz and the Rear MugGuard at muckynutz.com.
Find out more about The King’s Awards for Enterprise on GOV.UK.

title: Putting policy into practice at the International Maritime Organisation (IMO)

content.content: To mark the International Maritime Organisation’s (IMO’s) World Maritime Day we’re showing how the Maritime and Coastguard Agency (MCA) puts policy into practice.

Empowering maritime excellence comes hand in hand with our work at the IMO, where MCA colleagues represent the UK in discussions on international shipping regulation at multiple committee and sub-committee meetings throughout the year.
The most recent IMO sub-committee, CCC (Carriage of Cargoes and Containers), was held in London from 14 to 18 September with the aim of improving international safety regulations on:
John Booth, Future Propulsion and Fuel Safety Team Leader, and Shiv Ralhan, Fuel Propulsion and Fuel Safety Lead, represented the MCA.
Shiv said:
A week at the IMO, from seminars to group discussions
Alongside its core aims, an IMO sub-committee aims to spark debate and inspire delegates. Here’s what was on the agenda for the September meeting to achieve that:
Seminars
Networking
Group discussions
The following topics were discussed:

The committee focused on amendments to mandatory regulations (including the International Code of Safety for Ships using gases or other low-flashpoint fuels (IGF), the International Maritime Solid Bulk Cargoes Code (IMSBC) and International Maritime Dangerous Goods (IMDG) Code) and the development of safety and regulatory frameworks to support the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions from ships using new technologies and alternative fuels.

The team came away from the committee having finalised the interim guidelines for the safety of ships using methyl/ethyl alcohol fuels and made significant progress on the guidelines for ships using onboard carbon capture and storage systems.

Contributing to these events leads to important changes like those outlined above. It also acts as a focal point to the team's work throughout the year and supports the UK's objectives to improve maritime safety and environmental protection, benefiting our seafarers, local communities, the economy, and international peers.
About World Maritime Day

World Maritime Day was first established in 1978 by the IMO and is celebrated annually to focus attention on the importance of shipping safety, security and the marine environment. It also emphasises a particular aspect of the IMO’s work each year.
The Red Ensign and the IMO’s flag will fly at the MCA’s headquarters in Southampton in honour of World Maritime Day.

title: Driving test booking changes – 3 months on

content.content: As you will know, we've made some big changes to the driving test booking system this year. We brought these in to tackle exploitation, improve fairness and give more control to learner drivers, because genuine learners deserve a fair shot at getting a test slot.

This month marks 3 months since the last of these measures came into force and we're beginning to see the impact of the changes. We promised we'd update you at this point to tell you what the data is saying, so that's what I'm going to do.
Better data is giving us a clearer picture of demand

As our Chief Executive, Beverley Warmington, highlighted in a previous blog post, we're now publishing median waiting times data alongside our existing waiting-time measure. This follows a recommendation from the National Audit Office (NAO) to provide a fuller picture of learners’ actual experiences.
We are also publishing 2 related, but distinct, measures.

The first is slot availability. This shows the proportion of appointments within the 24-week booking window that are still available to book at a particular point in time. We publish this data at national, regional and test centre level, providing transparency on where capacity is available and helping us identify areas where demand continues to outstrip supply.

At the start of September, 11.86% of appointments across Great Britain were available to book. This was the joint-highest level since November 2024. On 1 September 2026, there were also around 50,000 more available tests than on 1 September 2025.

The second measure looks back at the tests completed during each month and shows the number and proportion that were booked and taken within different 7-week bands. It ranges from tests booked and taken within 7 weeks to those where more than 24 weeks passed between booking and the test taking place.

This is not a measure of how many slots were available on one particular day. It tells us about the actual experience of learners who took their test during that month. Publishing it nationally, regionally and by test centre helps show how experiences differ across Great Britain and how those patterns change over time.

No single measure tells the whole story. Looking at waiting times, current slot availability and learners’ completed-test experiences together give us a more rounded picture of demand and capacity. Better data does not reduce waiting times by itself, but it helps us target examiner recruitment, deployment and other interventions where they can make the greatest difference.
More tests are being conducted
Although we are not yet where we want to be, there is clear progress in our testing capacity.

We conducted 165,449 car driving tests in August, the highest number conducted in any August since records began in 2007. This brought the total number of tests conducted during the last 12 months to August to more than 2.13 million, the highest rolling 12-month total on record. Between April 2026 and August 2026, we have conducted over 906,000 tests, 15.5% more than during the same period last year.

This increased delivery has been supported by growth in our examiner workforce. In August, we had 1,605 full-time equivalent driving examiners able to deliver tests. That was 160 more than in August 2025, an increase of 11.1%, and our highest examiner capacity since November 2017.

Recruitment is only part of the picture. The increase in tests reflects the combined effect of recruitment and training, overtime working, improved workforce planning and targeted operational activity. We are increasingly using demand and capacity information at test-centre level to decide where recruitment and deployment will have the greatest impact.

The guidance on eyesight checks during driving tests is also being updated, meaning tests can now be booked during periods of poor natural light, as long as suitable artificial lighting is available for the learner to complete the eyesight check fairly. The legal eyesight requirement hasn't changed.
Improving pass rates

The latest figures also show that the pass rate remained above 50% for a ninth consecutive month. Thank you for the work you do to help pupils prepare properly and choose the right time to take their test.
What else we’re doing

We're also testing additional ways to help learners make the most of their appointments. This includes trialling reminder messages aimed at reducing avoidable non-attendance and ensuring valuable test slots are used effectively.

Alongside our existing workforce planning activity, we continue to explore targeted deployments of examiner resource into areas experiencing the greatest demand pressures. This supports our aim of achieving the greatest reduction in waiting times possible with the resource available.
Learners' behaviour is beginning to change

One of the aims of the booking changes was to make booking patterns reflect genuine learner demand more closely. Previously, some appointments were booked at test centres where the learner did not intend to take the test and were then moved elsewhere. This made it harder to understand local demand and could reduce access for learners who genuinely wanted to use those centres.

It is still early and we need to monitor the evidence over a longer period before drawing firm conclusions. However, we are seeing signs consistent with the intended direction of travel. Test availability has increased, including around 50,000 more appointments being available on 1 September 2026 than a year earlier. Availability is also becoming more visible outside the areas where demand was previously concentrated, although the position remains uneven across Great Britain.

The changes have reduced the scope for speculative movement by restricting learners to 2 booking changes, giving learners control of booking and managing their own test and limiting the locations to which an appointment can be moved. These controls are intended to reduce placeholder bookings and make the location of booked tests a better reflection of where learners genuinely intend to take them. This will give us a clearer view of which areas have the highest demand, allowing us to better manage and focus driving examiner resources.

We should be clear about what the evidence can and cannot yet show. Increased availability will also reflect the higher number of tests being provided, so it cannot be attributed solely to changed booking behaviour. We will continue to assess booking movements, changes, swaps and local availability before reaching firmer conclusions about the long-term behavioural effect of the reforms.
Making sure tests reach genuine learners

Fairness remains at the heart of the changes. Most learners use the booking system appropriately, but where there is evidence that an individual or organisation is trying to gain an unfair advantage or manage tests outside the rules, we will act.

Since the learner-only booking rules were introduced, we have been identifying and cancelling tests booked or managed in breach of those rules. More than 1,300 tests have been cancelled to date. We are also continuing to restrict online booking access where activity appears inconsistent with genuine personal use of the service.

Enforcement is not just about the number of accounts restricted or tests cancelled. Its purpose is to deter misuse, make automated and bulk activity harder to operate at scale and protect fair access for genuine learners. Where we have evidence that bookings breach the law or our terms and conditions, we will take appropriate action.
Keeping up the momentum

Three months is still early and waiting times remain higher than we want. Learners’ experiences also continue to vary considerably between locations. But the direction of travel is encouraging: we are conducting more tests, have more examiner capacity, are seeing greater appointment availability and now have better evidence to target our work.

We will continue publishing the data and being open about where progress is being made and where challenges remain. Our focus remains on reducing waiting times and creating a booking service that works fairly for genuine learners and the instructors supporting them.

title: Helping buyers and homeowners understand a property’s planning potential

content.content: PlanningHub joined the Geovation Accelerator Programme in March 2024. The programme, backed by HM Land Registry and Ordnance Survey, provides geospatial and PropTech start-ups with grant funding and 12 months of support, encouraging the innovative use of our data to benefit the property market, society and the economy.
Making planning decisions easier
Have you ever wondered whether a property could be extended before you buy it? Or perhaps been asked about planning permissions as a property professional?
Many people feel baffled when trying to understand planning rules and restrictions which can feel complex, fragmented and difficult to interpret.
That's exactly the challenge PlanningHub was created to solve - our goal is to make planning information easier to access and to act on.

The idea for PlanningHub came from my experience as an architect. Even for a simple householder project, answering questions such as Do I need planning permission? or What are my chances of getting approval? can involve searching multiple websites, interpreting complex planning rules and reviewing past planning decisions.
Creating a more transparent property market
So how does PlanningHub help exactly? We help people to understand a property's planning potential before investing significant time, money or professional fees.
We combine planning expertise with responsible artificial intelligence (AI) and trusted data sources to provide clear, property-specific planning information that people can understand and act on.

Our Householder Planning Permission Report examines the property’s location and project details and breaks down all the planning rules, restrictions, and past applications relevant to a property. Presented in an easy-to-read format, the report highlights key planning considerations, approved and rejected applications, and a checklist of documents needed for your planning application.
Helping buyers and homeowners make informed decisions

For someone buying a home, it helps answer questions such as whether an extension is likely to be possible and whether there are planning constraints that could affect future plans. It also gives buyers a clearer picture of a property's development potential before they exchange contracts.

For homeowners who already own a property, the report provides a clear starting point before investing in architects, designers or planning consultants. It highlights planning constraints, explains relevant policies and identifies similar planning applications nearby, helping people understand the planning context before taking the next step.
We also analyse planning activity around the property, giving users visibility of nearby developments that may influence future views, traffic, privacy or the overall enjoyment of their home.
How Geovation helped us grow

PlanningHub joined the Geovation Accelerator Programme in 2024 to accelerate the development of our products and learn from others transforming the property sector through technology. The programme gave us invaluable mentoring, industry connections and the opportunity to work closely with HM Land Registry and the wider PropTech community. It reinforced our belief that trusted public data can unlock practical solutions for everyday property decisions.
The role of HM Land Registry data

HM Land Registry data is fundamental to our products. Title information and indicative property boundaries provide the foundation for our reports. We combine this with planning, geographic and environmental datasets while also highlighting restrictive covenants (legal restrictions on a property) that may influence future development, something that is often overlooked during the property buying process. Together, these data sources allow us to present complex planning information in a way that is practical, trustworthy and relevant to a specific property.
Some of our successes
Our Householder Planning Permission Reports are now reaching thousands of homeowners and property buyers and are available through multiple platforms and partners.

Our customers include homeowners, developers, estate agents, conveyancers and local planning authorities, all of whom face the challenge of navigating planning information spread across multiple sources.

Since taking part in the Geovation Accelerator Programme, we have also been working with a number of local planning authorities, including Tower Hamlets, Enfield and Barking and Dagenham, in deploying digital technology and AI to improve planning processes.
What comes next

Looking ahead, we want buyers to be able to understand a property's development potential just as easily as they can check its energy rating or flood risk. We believe that giving people better planning intelligence earlier leads to better decisions, fewer surprises and a more transparent property market.

title: What good delivery means to us

content.content: The digital delivery community in the department is thriving. Across different teams, professions and directorates, we found ourselves returning to many of the same conversations about what good delivery looks like. As a group of Heads of Delivery, we wanted to capture those shared beliefs in one place, so we created our Principles of Delivery.

These are a set of 9 clear, tangible things to practise, to aim towards, to remember and acknowledge. They were co-written quickly, over the space of a few days to help limit the perfectionism that creeps in when something is important.

While our teams use different methods, tools and delivery approaches, we believe these principles are widely applicable. They focus on behaviours and mindsets rather than specific roles or frameworks.

We've described them simply as a set of principles to support consistent, effective delivery across the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG), regardless of directorate. They’re for everyone doing and delivering things. They're deliberately independent of role, grade or location. They’re for us all and it feels good to be sharing them more widely now too.
These principles are now part of our internal MHCLG Digital Manual, where they sit alongside other guidance and resources that support teams across the department.
We don’t want these sat around collecting electronic dust, instead they’re designed to be discussed and pointed back to.
MHCLG Principles of Delivery
1. Be pragmatic, focus on what matters
Delivery is about achieving outcomes, not following process for its own sake.
Aim for 'good enough' where appropriate, rather than over-engineering.
Use process, tools and documentation to support delivery, not slow it down.
2. Happy people = good delivery
Pay attention to team wellbeing alongside delivery. Sustainable pace matters massively.
Create an environment where people can do their best work and feel recognised for it.
Teams that feel supported, valued and psychologically safe are often happier and more motivated, and deliver better outcomes.
Treat people with respect regardless of role, contract or grade. Focus on outcomes over hierarchy.
3. Keep things open, including any bad news
Openness builds trust and helps teams make better decisions, especially when things aren't going to plan. Share challenges and setbacks early.
Create a culture where people feel safe to raise problems, challenge assumptions and ask for help.
Be honest about what's working and what isn't. Deal with issues rather than hoping they'll resolve themselves.
4. Share work often, in a way that works for others
Making work visible helps teams spot issues earlier, build confidence and avoid duplication.
Share progress regularly using formats that work for your audience (for example, drop-ins, show and tells, email updates).
Prioritise good over perfect. Early visibility is more valuable than late, finished outputs.
5. Plan to deliver, adapt when needed
Set a clear direction and priorities, without over-specifying upfront.
Adapt quickly as you learn. Plans should enable delivery, not constrain it.
6. Make risks visible and actionable
Surfacing risks early allows teams to act before they become issues. We should all capture and share risks openly, with clear ownership and next steps.
Focus on action – what are we doing about it, and by when?
7. Work in a rhythm and cadence that's right for the team
Consistent ways of working help teams stay aligned and make progress sustainable.
Set a regular delivery rhythm (for example, stand-ups, show and tells, retros) that supports the team’s work, and review it regularly, especially as the team changes.
Keep meetings proportionate. Useful and lightweight over time-consuming and process-heavy.
8. Everything can't be a priority, help people choose
Clear prioritisation helps teams focus their effort where it has the most impact.
Be explicit about what matters most, and what can wait or stop.
Support teams to make trade-offs, especially when demand exceeds capacity.
Break work into small, manageable pieces to enable progress and reduce risk.
9. Make time for the delivery community
Strong connections across teams improve consistency, capability and shared learning.
Reuse existing tools, patterns and approaches where possible rather than reinventing.
Create opportunities for delivery colleagues to connect, share experience and solve problems together.
Contribute back and share what’s working and what isn’t, to help others.

title: Connections count: Building trust with families to improve attendance

content.content: As a new term begins, school corridors are buzzing with energy. New pupils, staff and families are getting to know each other, and others are reconnecting after the summer break.  The ultimate lever to secure strong attendance is building trust and warm, strong relationships with families right from day one. Schools and parents share a common goal: happy, healthy children who feel they belong, and achieve their potential. Rooting your approach in this common ground can help build genuine partnerships with families.
Building trust

Findings from the A Crisis of Disengagement report highlight a massive shift in parental attitudes since the pandemic. Many families feel a real disconnect, they say that school communications are transactional and not supportive. The report notes that the attendance crisis is not simply about poor choices or behaviour, it’s a crisis of disengagement. When pupils lose their connection to routines, friends, and trusted adults, attendance declines.

A ‘Support First’ approach is essential to spot attendance barriers. Transactional approaches simply don't uncover deep-rooted causes like poverty, anxiety, home pressures, or SEND. Real progress happens when staff listen to understand a family's barriers and figure out the right support together before patterns become entrenched.

The data you have at your disposal might help you identify a family experiencing some of these barriers, but it’s the family and individuals behind the data you need to build trust and relationships with, so you can work together on solutions. It sounds easy, and I know it’s not simple, but during recent school visits, I’ve seen fantastic examples of relationship building in action:
Leading with warmth

Warm welcomes at the school gate and classroom doors set an inviting tone, and reassured parents and children. Practical touches like extended morning drop-off and staggered starts quelled anxiety, while Year 11s forming a guard-of-honour made Year 7s feel instantly welcome and safe. Some schools used walking buses or minibus pick-ups to collect anxious pupils and those whose families need support. Several schools ran uniform exchanges over summer and on INSET days, so everyone felt ready on day one.
Investing time

Schools gave new pupils extra tutor time during week one to build trust and settle into routines. Others hosted visits where parents explored classrooms, met teachers, and sampled school lunches. Several have scheduled residential visits during autumn term to help pupils connect with peers and staff outside the classroom early on.
Rethinking messaging

Many leaders used the DfE guide ‘communicating with parents about attendance’ to prepare families for a smooth return. The guide offers practical advice on how to frame attendance messages, templates for you to adapt, and other resources such as a communications calendar to help you plan across the school year and animations to use with parents. It emphasises the need to focus on missed days, lessons, and experiences not percentages.
Being curious and listening

Leaders I’ve met have questioned what the data was telling them and used it to start a conversation rather than jumping to conclusions. They used Year 6 attendance data from VYED to spot vulnerable families and then worked with them ahead of the transition. They spent time listening to understand each family's barriers then built collaborative plans with them.

I hope this blog has sparked a few ideas that might help your school continue to improve the way you build and maintain relationships with parents and pupils. You may also find these case study videos valuable - Attendance and Behaviour Hub schools discussing how they have successfully engaged parents and worked collaboratively with families on attendance.

If you are looking for more information, you can access further attendance guidance and toolkits. If you’d like to access sector-led, practical support, and learn directly from schools already achieving strong outcomes, consider joining the Attendance and Behaviour Hubs Programme.

When schools and parents work together around the shared goal of helping children feel happy, included and able to do well, attendance is more likely to improve.

title: Building cyber resilience in the UK one step at a time: a spotlight on a Defence Cyber Certification Certifying Body

content.content: The Ministry of Defence have asked all industry partners to achieve Level 0 of the Defence Cyber Certification (DCC) by 31st December 2026, which includes a requirement for obtaining Cyber Essentials for all applicable business-critical systems within scope.

The cyber landscape is rapidly changing, and supply chain security has never been more important. The recently announced Cyber Resilience Pledge and the forthcoming National Cyber Action Plan (NCAP) and Cyber Security and Resilience Bill (CSRB) are asking all organisations to reassess their cyber resilience and harden their critical supply chains. The DCC is the next step to a more secure defence industry. The UK needs to ensure that Defence and its partners are protected.

To support this transition, suppliers must be encouraged to work towards this objective and to ensure that any subcontractor timescales are set appropriately, where higher levels of certification are required at lower tiers in the supply chain.
The Ministry of Defence would like to give a spotlight to RightCue, a Certifying Body for IASME, who are helping organisations to achieve DCC.
RightCue's biggest achievement is delivering the very first Level 1 certification.
RightCue's Founder, Yogesh Agarwal, talks through his experience of becoming a Certifying Body for the DCC.

Our decision was driven by both the needs of our clients and a commitment to strengthening cyber resilience across the UK's defence supply chain. Having supported defence suppliers with Cyber Essentials, Cyber Essentials Plus and DCPP requirements for many years, we saw organisations seeking guidance when the MOD introduced DCC Levels 0 to 3.

The transition from CSMv3 to CSMv4 aligned closely with our expertise, with the focus expanding beyond protecting MOD Identifiable Information to improving organisational security, resilience, governance and risk management.

We were also involved in developing the DCC scheme alongside IASME, helping to ensure the controls and guidance reflected the practical challenges faced by defence suppliers. As an NCSC Assured Cyber Security Consultancy and Assured Service Provider, CREST accredited, ISO 27001 certified becoming a Certifying Body was a natural next step.

It enables us to help organisations strengthen their cyber resilience, meet defence sector requirements and contribute to the wider goal of protecting Defence, its supply chains and ultimately the UK's national security in an increasingly challenging cyber landscape.

The first step is becoming an IASME Cyber Essentials Certification Body. The organisation and its assessors must be based in the UK or Crown Dependencies. Assessors must meet IASME's qualification requirements and complete DCC training and assessments for the levels they wish to deliver. The training covers Def Stan 05-138 Issue 4 and focuses heavily on assessment scoping, which is one of the most important aspects of the certification process.
Once approved, IASME licenses and publishes the organisation as a Certifying Body for the levels it is qualified to assess.
RightCue qualified across all four DCC levels.
While the process is accessible to organisations of different sizes, success depends on having assessors who can apply the standard consistently and make evidence-based decisions with confidence.

Although Level 0 contains only three controls, preparation can take longer than many organisations expect because Cyber Essentials is a prerequisite. The starting point should be ensuring Cyber Essentials is in place and that its scope aligns with the intended DCC scope. In our experience, scoping is the single biggest challenge for applicants and the most common cause of delays.

Organisations should clearly identify the systems, processes and business functions that are essential for the organisation to operate securely and resiliently, not just those directly supporting MOD-related activities. This includes understanding where data is stored, who is responsible for managing key assets, and ensuring all critical business systems are considered within scope. Completing this exercise early makes the assessment process significantly smoother.

We also recommend making use of the free guidance available from IASME. There is a wealth of information available to help organisations understand the requirements, define an appropriate scope, and prepare effectively before engaging a Certifying Body

Most importantly, start early. With the MOD's Level 0 deadline approaching, organisations that leave preparation until the final months may struggle to secure assessment capacity and complete any remediation work required.
Not necessarily. DCC is a risk-based framework and organisations should focus on achieving the level required by their contract and cyber risk profile.

There is a significant difference in effort between the certification levels, with higher levels requiring greater maturity, more evidence and additional assurance activities. While Level 3 demonstrates a high degree of cyber resilience, it may not represent the best investment for every organisation.

We encourage businesses to view their assigned DCC level as a minimum requirement. If future contracts are likely to require higher levels, then building towards them through a planned security roadmap makes sense.
The ultimate objective should be improving security and resilience, not simply obtaining the highest certification level available.

Start with your assessors. DCC assessments require expertise in governance, risk management and organisational resilience as well as technical cyber security controls. It is also important to be realistic about which certification levels your organisation can support. Levels 1 to 3 are significantly more demanding than Level 0 and require greater assessor capacity, more evidence review and, in some cases, site visits and security-cleared personnel.

Consistency is equally important. As a relatively new scheme, DCC relies on suppliers receiving the same outcome regardless of which Certifying Body conducts the assessment. Maintaining that consistency is critical to the credibility of the scheme.

Finally, engage with industry. Building relationships with organisations, trade bodies and suppliers helps develop trust and provides valuable insight into the challenges facing the defence supply chain.

One of our proudest achievements was delivering the UK's first DCC Level 1 certification. It demonstrated both our preparedness for the scheme and our ability to assess organisations against the more demanding certification levels.

However, some of our most impactful work happens before an assessment even begins. We regularly help organisations identify and correct scoping issues that would otherwise result in delays, additional costs or failed assessments.

We are particularly proud of the support we provide to SMEs. Many smaller suppliers start with limited cyber security resources and little experience of assurance frameworks. Helping them achieve certification and improve their cyber resilience is one of the most rewarding aspects of our work.
Ultimately, our biggest success is making DCC practical and achievable for organisations across the defence supply chain, regardless of their size or level of cyber maturity.
We will be sharing more of these DCC stories as the deadline approaches.

title: Why our forests matter to us more than ever before

content.content: The UK is one of the least forested nations in Europe and one of the most nature depleted countries in the world. A recent report investigated the value of forest biodiversity in Great Britain, and found that creating and managing more woodland would bring huge economic benefits to society.

The report also found that households in Great Britain strongly support increasing species diversity in the country’s forests, deeming the benefits from creating new forests or improving existing forests as significant.
The 2025 Value of Forest Biodiversity in Great Britain report

For over a decade, people making the case for woodlands have been working with outdated figures on the value of forest biodiversity. The 2025 Value of Forest Biodiversity in Great Britain report, commissioned by the Forestry Commission and funded by the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affair’s Nature for Climate Fund provides an up-to-date picture of the benefits our woodlands and forests deliver, reflecting today’s woodlands, economy and public support.
Measuring forest biodiversity

The report values the cultural benefit to society of improvements in forest biodiversity. Via surveys, focus groups and one-to-one interviews, the public were asked about their willingness to pay for improvements to forest biodiversity and woodland creation.
The benefits include:
Cultural benefits

The Climate Change Committee (CCC) established under the Climate Change Act 2008, set out targets of having approximately 1 million hectares of newly planted forests by 2050, and forests in improved condition.

To achieve this, approximately 30,000 hectares of new woodland would need to be planted annually in the UK until 2050. For context, a forest cover of 17–19%, as suggested by the CCC, has not been seen in England since before the Domesday survey in 1086.

This study finds that if we hit these targets, it would result in up to £8.3 billion per year in cultural benefits to UK households. This value is in addition to the indirect benefits forests provide, including carbon sequestration, timber production, flood management, water filtration and air purification.
Access to nature and landscapes

Since the COVID-19 pandemic, there has been a significant boost in awareness of the importance of access to nature and landscapes. In 2025, 70% of the public reported having visited forests or woodlands in the last few years, compared to 56% in 2015.1

Greater concerns about environmental deterioration and increased understanding about the importance of nature were also cited by the public as reasons for wanting to see an improvement in forest biodiversity.
A growing average value for general forest biodiversity improvement

The national average value set out for general forest biodiversity improvement has risen to approximately £5,400 per hectare per year, applied over a 60-year period. This value includes the importance of public places and the enjoyment of spotting forest wildlife, as well as improvements to recreation and area amenities.

When compared to previous studies, this represents a significant increase in value to the public of forest biodiversity over the past 20 years, despite cost-of-living challenges. Previous studies such as Willis et al. (2003) reported values of between £195 per hectare per year for conifer woodland, and £2,040 per hectare per year for ancient woodland (in 2024 prices).

This new report includes a household ‘willingness to pay’ figure of £304 per household, per year, for achieving a national forest cover increase of 1 million hectares. It also includes a range of combined non-use and use values for specific levels of forest biodiversity improvement ranging from £3,400 per hectare per year for forest biodiversity improvement from ‘minimal to low’ species diversity, to £8,600 per hectare per year, for ‘minimal to high’ species diversity improvement (applied over a 60-year time period).
A view to plant more trees

The evidence is clear: the public wants more forests, and richer ones. This research gives us the most up-to-date and robust picture yet of just how much that ambition is worth – not only in pounds but in the ‘connection’ people feel to the natural world.

For councils making planning decisions, land managers considering whether to pursue woodland creation schemes, and community groups wanting greener local spaces, this report provides the evidence. The values set out here can be used in a range of analyses including business cases and cost-benefit analysis, to demonstrate the social value that comes from investing in nature.

The report provides clear economic evidence of public support and social value for increased woodland creation and forest biodiversity across the UK. The ambition to reverse the UK's status as one of the least forested and most nature-depleted nations in Europe will require action at every level: national policy, local planning and individual land management decisions.
This report equips everyone involved in that effort with the evidence to make the case so we can plant the right trees, in the right places, to benefit future generations.

title: SFI26 Window 2: an update

content.content: Farmers have had a difficult 2026: navigating the impact of extreme drought and hot weather, the ongoing rise in Bluetongue virus cases, and input price rises from the Middle East conflict.

The exceptional demand for the Sustainable Farming Incentive (SFI) demonstrates farmers’ desire to invest in the environment, because healthy soils and thriving habitats are fundamental for farm profitability, productivity, sustainability & resilience.

In anticipation of high demand, Ministers decided to allocate an additional £20m to Window 2, on top of the £50m announced by the Prime Minister in August, so that we could fund as many agreements as possible.

We have therefore allocated a total of £310m to new agreements across both application windows in SFI26, £253m through Window 2. These agreements will invest a total of £930m in environmentally sustainable farming over the next 3 years.
This year we ensured small farms and those new to Environmental Land Management (ELM) revenue schemes were prioritised - with an exclusive first window earlier in the summer.

Previously a quarter of SFI funding headed to just 4% of farms making claims. That is why we capped SFI26 agreements at £100,000 per year. We also reduced some payment rates for a number of actions in order to ensure the available budget could stretch further.
Still, we know some farmers who wanted to join SFI26 will be disappointed not to have secured an agreement this year.

In keeping with the commitments made in the Farming Roadmap 2050, we plan to offer an SFI scheme in 2027. We will look to open the 2027 offer as early as possible to ensure farmers can access funding.

We are ready to look at how we can improve SFI for next year – continuing our close work with farmers and stakeholders by listening to experiences and learning lessons from this window. As part of this, we are exploring alternatives to a first come, first served application process for SFI in 2027.

Farmers can still apply for Countryside Stewardship Higher Tier (CSHT) funding via the Expression of Interest (EOI) process. You can submit EOIs for woodland improvement and agroforestry, as well as new single-focus agreements for management of species rich grassland and scheduled monument management.
Next steps for SFI26

The RPA is working through queries from farmers and agents received via email as quickly as possible They have already returned calls for anyone who rang yesterday before Window 2 closed for applications.
Now Window 2 has closed, the Rural Payments Agency (RPA) will process applications as quickly and efficiently as possible.

As a reminder, if you started an application but did not submit it before Window 2 closed, you will not be able to submit it. This is because we closed the window when we had enough applications to allocate the full Window 2 budget.
We will allow two small ‘exception groups’, who contacted the RPA before Window 2 closed, to continue with their applications. They are:

The RPA will contact ‘started but not submitted’ Window 2 farmers in due course to confirm whether their applications will be withdrawn, or if they’re in an exception group and can continue with their application.
Applications are processed in the order in which they were submitted. Some applications require additional checks and can therefore take longer to assess.
We will provide an update on when successful applicants can expect to receive their agreement offer in due course.
SFI26 Window 2 statistics at a glance
We are conducting a final analysis of Window 2 application statistics. We will publish an official statistics release at 9:30am on Friday 25 September.
Numbers have been rounded to help illustrate the overall picture and should be treated as indicative rather than exact.

These figures are based on the applications we received at the point we closed Window 2 for applications, and the information provided by applicants at the point of application. They do not reflect final agreement figures, as applications are still being processed and the RPA handles farmers in the exception groups. As a result, final contracted uptake, including the actions selected, areas covered and associated values, may differ from these initial figures.
Applications
Approximately 12,200 applications were submitted during Window 2. Against our budget of £253 million, this means the average agreement value applied for was approximately £20,700.

More than 8,800 of those farmers have an ELM revenue agreement expiring on or before 28 February 2027. The new functionality in the SFI26 application service allowed farmers to start an application early for the full range of available SFI26 actions on land in an existing ELM revenue agreement before that agreement ends. Previously, these farmers would have had to wait until their existing agreement ended before being able to do this.
Over 1,100 farmers who applied in Window 2 are farmers who don’t have an existing ELM revenue agreement.
Top 5 actions
Applicants selected actions across all 14 SFI26 action groups, reflecting the flexibility of the scheme and the diversity of farming businesses taking part. The most popular actions were:
CLIG3: Manage grassland with very low nutrient inputs – over 7,400 applications

The benefits of this action extend beyond biodiversity. When established alongside cropped land, species-rich grasslands can support the natural processes that underpin resilient food production. Flower-rich habitats provide resources for pollinators and other beneficial insects, while diverse vegetation offers shelter for species that contribute to natural pest regulation. These areas can also slow surface water movement, reducing soil and nutrient losses and helping to retain valuable resources within the farmed landscape.
CHRW2: Manage hedgerows – over 4,300 applications

Well-managed hedgerows can support the natural processes that contribute to resilient food production. Flowering hedgerows provide resources for pollinating insects, while their shelter and habitat benefits encourage populations of beneficial invertebrates that can contribute to natural pest regulation and integrated pest management. Hedgerows can also help reduce wind erosion, slow surface water movement and improve the retention of soil and nutrients within the farmed landscape.
CSAM3: Herbal leys – over 3,300 applications
This action aims to maintain an established herbal ley containing a diverse mixture of grasses, legumes, herbs and wildflowers that provide varied root structures throughout the soil profile.

The ley should include areas of flowering plants from late spring through the summer months, supporting biodiversity and providing valuable resources for pollinators and other wildlife. The purpose of this mixture is to produce a high volume of forage while minimising the need for inorganic fertilisers, improving resilience to drought, and helping to enhance and maintain the soil’s structure, carbon content, biological activity and overall fertility.
CAHL2: Winter bird food on arable and horticultural land – over 2,600 applications

This action supports the growth of a mix of seed-bearing crops that supply vital small seeds from late autumn through late winter for species like finches, buntings, sparrows, and partridges. The seed mix also encourages summer flowering plants that provide nectar and pollen for beneficial insects, including bumblebees, solitary bees, butterflies, and hoverflies. It also supports natural predators of crop pests through an integrated pest management (IPM) approach when strips or blocks are planted close to cropped areas.
CIPM4: No use of insecticide on arable crops and permanent crops – over 2,600 applications

By encouraging no insecticide usage, this SFI action protects beneficial insects like bees, butterflies, and natural pest predators, stops chemical residues from running off into nearby streams, rivers, and groundwater or drifting into the air.

title: Sewage detectives: how UKHSA is using wastewater to track common viruses and emerging threats

content.content: The wastewater that we send from our toilets towards sewage treatment plants every day is potentially rich in data about our health. For the past 4 years, UKHSA has been monitoring wastewater across England for signs of polio, and over the past year has been testing new technologies to detect other potential threats. The next phase of the programme – made possible by a £3 million investment from the UK Integrated Security Fund (ISF) - will expand our capabilities and enable us to publish new data.
What is PRISM, and why does it matter?

Pathogen Risk Intelligence through Surveillance and Modelling (PRISM) is UKHSA's expanding wastewater and environmental surveillance programme, designed to detect a wide range of pathogens that could affect public health.

What makes PRISM different from traditional wastewater surveillance is that it isn't limited to a single pathogen. Instead, one sample of wastewater can be tested for many different threats at once. This gives significantly more value from every sample collected.
What has the programme achieved over the past year?

The team's biggest achievement has been proving this multi-pathogen approach actually works. Before PRISM, wastewater testing in government tended to focus on one target at a time. Now, UKHSA has demonstrated that a single sample can support public health surveillance, biosecurity monitoring and tracking of antimicrobial resistance simultaneously.

This proof of concept has opened doors that were previously closed. UKHSA is now working with government and academic partners to realise the vision of ‘sample once – test many’. Exploring how wastewater surveillance could support their specific needs, from targeted testing to detecting diseases arising from interactions between humans, animals and the environment.

The programme's surveillance network currently covers the wastewater of around 25 million people across England, a scale made possible by building on infrastructure already in place for the UK's polio elimination programme.
What is currently being monitored?

Right now, PRISM is testing for a range of pathogens including norovirus, enterovirus, flu A, flu B, rhinovirus, RSV and COVID-19 identifiers. The current approach detects presence or absence, rather than tracking trends over time. In parallel, PRISM is also taking a less targeted approach that can detect any or all pathogens in a sample without needing to know beforehand what specific organism is present. This is vital if we are to better detect new or unusual pathogens.

One area where PRISM is already delivering practical value is norovirus, the winter vomiting bug. The programme can track norovirus strains circulating across the country, helping build a clearer picture of the pressures facing the NHS each winter.
What's changing in the coming year?

New investment is enabling the programme to build new technology-driven capabilities, allowing for PRISM to unlock more value from wastewater. We are adding new sites, increasing our coverage and improving our ability to detect pathogens that were previously hard to detect. The programme - through new automation technologies - is now better able to scale to demands and make these new approaches more accessible to others. A key outcome for the programme, is bridging the gap between data and action. Using these new technologies, and data analytics, we can now build a system that goes from sample, to data, to insight and action.
Before this data is used more widely, it will be tested and compared against other technologies to check its reliability and accuracy, since different pathogens behave differently in wastewater.
What new pathogens will PRISM look for?

The programme has confirmed a set of new targets to prioritise for the coming year, taking advantage of one of our capabilities, chosen to reflect the range of threats the team wants to be ready for. These include diseases with existing elimination goals, such as mpox and measles, alongside emerging threats like avian influenza, Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever, West Nile virus, Lassa fever and Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus (MERS-CoV).

The list also includes hepatitis A and hepatitis E, and 2 priorities in the fight against antimicrobial resistance: Candidozyma auris and hypervirulent Klebsiella pneumoniae, both of increasing concern to public health experts worldwide.
These targets have been selected to strengthen preparedness and support earlier detection of potential public health threats, rather than because they are currently widespread in the UK.
Building the capability to detect these targets earlier means the country will be better prepared for emerging threats.
What does the future hold?

Beyond new pathogens, over the coming year PRISM will explore targeted surveillance in new environments such as targeted hospital wastewater sites and high-footfall locations, including transport hubs, alongside exploratory work on air surveillance. This work will help assess where environmental surveillance could add most value.
The team is also exploring how this data could support hospitals directly, potentially helping to spot antimicrobial resistance outbreaks early and easing pressure on NHS beds.

Longer term, the ambition is for PRISM to become a permanent, business-as-usual capability within UKHSA, integrated with existing public health surveillance systems so that findings can directly inform decisions and protect communities across England.

title: A postcard from Darlington

content.content: As No10 North gathers momentum, I wanted to offer a perspective from the other side of the Pennines – the Darlington Economic Campus, or No11 North as the Chancellor recently put it.

HMT has traditionally been one of the most London-centric of government departments so the move over the last five years to have a fifth of our staff based in Darlington has been a big change. But when we began creating the Darlington Economic Campus (DEC) in 2021, we wanted to do more than just establish a new government office outside London. Instead we had a vision to work differently with the other departments based here and with our external partners in the region.

Since we launched, we have been co-located with eight other government departments and ALBs. We have deliberately organised ourselves as one campus rather than as a collection of separate organisations. We sit alongside one another, share events and communications, and bring together colleagues with different expertise to solve the country’s thorniest policy issues.

We have also forged new partnerships with local and regional government, local businesses and the third sector. Through initiatives like the Community Mission Challenge we have undertaken joint projects with Darlington Council; and every week we hold different events and workshops on key policy questions with external stakeholders.
Partnership is how we get better results

The way we work isn’t an accident. We work in partnership with other departments because the challenges we face do not fit neatly within departmental boundaries. Growth, skills, transport, housing… everything is connected. Bringing departments together helps us move beyond institutional silos and focus on the outcomes that matter.

Just as importantly, our strong external relationships with mayors, local authorities, universities and public service providers give our policy makers direct access to experience on the ground: what is working, where barriers remain, and how national decisions are felt in different communities.

We showed the difference this makes in the recent announcement that mayors would receive a share of income tax revenues. Thanks to our work in partnership with local stakeholders, we understand what will turn the dial for them in shifting power, funding and decision-making closer to their areas. As we work alongside No10 North and colleagues across the government on this agenda, these relationships will bear even more fruit.
Hearing different voices

For us at HM Treasury, one of the campus’s greatest strengths is the range of voices it has brought into the organisation. The vast majority of my colleagues in DEC have been recruited from the surrounding region, and most joined the civil service from other sectors having not worked in government before.

DEC provides an opportunity for people who previously wouldn’t have been able to work in policy roles in the civil service to do so. It brings in a much wider range of people, with different experiences and perspectives, to improve our advice to ministers and the services we provide the public and to make sure we better reflect the country we serve.

I often hear from colleagues who grew up in the North East that previously they thought they would have to move to London to work on the complex and cross-cutting issues that they do currently. And now that the campus has been established for a few years, we’re seeing that people can not only get a job where they are from thanks to DEC, they can build a career.

On the launch day of No 10 North, the Prime Minister addressed critics by saying, “it’s not just a new office”, and I agree. DEC - and No 10 North – may seem to the sceptical like surface level changes, but if we put the energy and commitment into building partnerships, empowering local colleagues, and getting everyone round the table, then we can change the way our country is wired.
So whether you call us the Darlington Economic Campus or No 11 North, what we do is the same: delivering the best advice and action for ministers and the country we serve.

title: Build once, benefit many: driving business case transformation across government, one (agile) step at a time
authors: Ellie Katona, Senior Interaction Designer, Digital Process Improvement team

content.content: A business case is a framework used by government to get approval to spend public money and ensure the delivery of public benefits. Our user research with people across several government departments showed that teams face similar challenges with business cases writing and approval. They are regarded as disproportionate, long-winded, unclear and difficult to both write and approve. Each department is investing time and resources into solving these same problems.

We in the Digital Process Improvement team at the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) like solving problems, and it doesn’t get more knotty than business cases (so far!). We’re a friendly bunch from across different backgrounds and disciplines, driven by a common goal of helping people do their jobs better, at MHCLG and across government.
Why reinvent the wheel when you can share the blueprint and the service? We have a huge opportunity here for proper, cross-government collaboration.
Sharing is caring

From the start of the project to improve the business case process, in partnership with our Approvals and Assurance team, our goal was to build something based on our guiding principles of putting people first, joining the dots and understanding data. Something robust, that could be 'plug and play' for any department who wanted help with their business case process.

We started with the triage service: a way for people to self-serve business case templates and guidance. People struggle to find the correct template, understand approvals and who to speak to, according to our discovery insights. In triage, people answer a few questions to find the template they need. They are also encouraged to partner with Finance and Commercial early on, fostering the idea that collaboration is key to a successful business case.

The Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (BIST) showed an interest in the work we were doing; there were many similarities with challenges but ultimately an appetite for change and exploration was welcome and we were able to share with policy and digital teams our triage service to 'steal with pride'.
What’s under the hood of the business case triage service?
Upshot

Sharing our journey so far with BIST has reinforced the value of collaboration across departments, particularly when tackling common challenges. By sharing approaches, lessons learned and reusable components, we can speed up delivery, focus resources where they add the greatest value and save time and money. Not just for MHCLG but across the entire government. Our work to transform the business case process continues as we build out the end-to-end service, and we’ll aim to share more about our progress. Who next? Arm's-length bodies? Let’s go!
Want your own triage service or want to learn more?
Get in touch! Find us at businesscaseproject@communities.gov.uk.

description: Business cases help government make decisions about spending public money and delivering public benefit. MHCLG’s Digital Process Improvement team is applying user-centred design to make the business case process simpler, reduce duplication and support better collaboration across government, starting with a reusable triage service.

title: Success builds on success for newts and developers

content.content: By Stephanie Bird-Halton, Director - National Delivery at Natural England

The 2025/26 Annual Monitoring Report for Natural England’s District Level Licensing (DLL) for great crested newts has just been published. This blog explores the successes so far and shows that the scheme is creating high quality habitat for great crested newts, while giving developers more certainty and speeding up planning decisions. Through the scheme more than 51,500 new homes and more than 15,000 hectares of developments have been enabled and over 4,747 compensation ponds created or restored. Overall, it proves that development and nature recovery can successfully work hand-in-hand.

In England great crested newts, known for their striking orange and black spotted bellies and the male's wavy crest along his back, are very important in our pond landscape. In the last century, though, there has been a sharp decline in the species mainly due to pond loss and intensive agriculture. Great crested newt populations are estimated to have declined by more than 40% since the start of the 20th century, while around two-thirds of ponds have been lost from our landscapes.

This has led to great crested newts being protected, with environmental regulations put in place to support their long-term future. To enable developers to more efficiently and effectively meet these regulations and to facilitate nature recovery across entire landscapes, District Level Licensing (DLL) for great crested newts was launched.

We have now published the 2025/26 Annual Monitoring Report for Natural England DLL and it demonstrates that the scheme continues to support nature recovery while giving developers greater certainty and helping local planning authorities (LPAs) progress planning applications more quickly.

DLL for great crested newts provides an alternative to the traditional sitebysite approach. Instead of surveying and protecting newts on site, developers can offset the evidence based predicted harm of their development by funding the creation of new ponds in places where newts are most likely to thrive, and the monitoring and maintenance of these for 25 years. General information about the  Natural England DLL scheme
The scheme aims to:

This Annual Monitoring Report sets out the outcomes of Natural England's DLL scheme for 2025 to 2026 and highlights key achievements since launch. Its findings are consistent with the first five-year evaluation report, published in early 2026. For more information on these results read our blog post: The First Five-Year Evaluations of Strategic Licensing for Great Crested Newts.
High‑quality habitat for newts

By 31 July 2026 4,611 compensation ponds had been created or restored through DLL. That’s 967,000 square meters of pond habit, with terrestrial habitat made available to newts by the ponds. The Annual Monitoring Report showed that:

Great crested newts use networks of ponds and the expectation of DLL is not for all compensation ponds to be used by newts at the same time. Some scheme areas are less than five years old and ponds have fewer than five-years monitoring data. We look forward to seeing outcomes of the scheme as the survey data grows.
Habitat delivery partners recall success

Under DLL, developer compensation includes the monitoring and maintenance of ponds for 25 years by our Habitat Delivery Body partners, including Wildlife Trusts and Farming & Wildlife Advisory Groups (FWAGs). Ponds which are restored under DLL must be completely unsuitable for great crested newts in their current condition, meeting criteria to ensure additional habitat is delivered.

A successful approach for nature and growth

The Annual Monitoring Report 2025/26 shows that District Level Licensing is working for nature and development. Thousands of new and restored ponds and habitats are providing vital spaces for great crested newts and other wildlife across the landscape.

title: SFI26: Window 2 now closed

content.content: Window 2 of the Sustainable Farming Incentive 2026 (SFI26) closed at 15:48 on Tuesday 22 September 2026. Thank you to everyone who took the time to submit an application.
We have seen strong interest in the scheme and are grateful to all those who chose to apply in this window.
If you receive an agreement offer, please make sure you accept it within 30 calendar days, or the offer will be withdrawn.

If you are not successful in getting an agreement, eligible farmers and land managers will have another opportunity to apply for the SFI in 2027. We will publish details on next year’s SFI offer in due course.
Processing times

Now Window 2 has closed, the Rural Payments Agency (RPA) will continue to process applications as quickly and efficiently as possible. It’s important to note that agreements will only be offered to eligible applications if sufficient budget remains.
Applications are processed in the order in which they were submitted. Some applications require additional checks and can therefore take longer to assess.
We will provide an update on when successful applicants can expect to receive their agreement offer in due course.
Started but not submitted applications

If you started an application but did not submit it before Window 2 closed, you will not be able to submit it. This is because we closed the window when we had enough applications to allocate the full Window 2 budget.
We will allow two small ‘exception groups’, who contacted the RPA before Window 2 closed, to continue with their applications. They are:

The RPA will contact ‘started but not submitted’ Window 2 farmers in due course to confirm whether their applications will be withdrawn, or they’re in an exception group and can continue with their application.
Farmers who didn’t apply for Window 2 may be eligible to apply for the SFI offer in 2027. We will publish more details in due course.
Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSSIs)
If you’ve applied for SFI26 on SSSI land, it’s important that you submit the required SSSI notice to get consent from Natural England as soon as possible.
The RPA cannot offer you an SFI26 agreement until you’ve done this.
Read section 10.1 ‘SSSI consent’ in the SFI26 scheme rules and guidance to find out how to do this.
Countryside Stewardship Higher Tier
Other funding opportunities remain available.
Countryside Stewardship (CSHT) remains open to new applicants. Those invited to apply by Natural England can secure 10-year agreements, combining 132 land management actions and capital grant items.

Additionally, the new Expression of Interest (EOI) process provides a simpler route into CSHT. You can submit EOIs for woodland improvement and agroforestry, as well as new single-focus agreements for management of species rich grassland and scheduled monument management.
SFI26 statistics at a glance
We will publish official statistics on SFI26 Window 2 agreement and action uptake in due course.
Please subscribe to the Farming Blog to receive an email notification when we publish these statistics.
On 9 September, we published official statistics on SFI26 Window 1 agreement and action uptake.

These figures are based on the applications we received in Window 1, and the information provided by applicants at the point of application. They do not reflect final agreement figures, as applications are still being processed.
SFI in 2027

title: Hobbit Day and the legacy of Middle-earth

content.content: September 22 marks the autumn equinox and for me, without fail, the start of my annual Gilmore Girls rewatch. However, this year Stars Hollow is not my first stop. I’ve decided to go down a very different road, “and the road goes ever and on”, for September 22 is Hobbit Day!
A tale of two birthdays

This date wasn't chosen at random either. September 22 is widely celebrated as the shared birthday of Bilbo and Frodo Baggins and was officially designated as Hobbit Day by the American Tolkien Society in 1978 as part of Tolkien Week.
Shall we go on an adventure

While Bilbo Baggins would probably have been happiest enjoying a quiet life in the Shire with a well-stocked pantry and no unexpected visitors, the world he helped inspire has become anything but quiet.

Nearly 90 years after The Hobbit was first published, Middle-earth, the fictional world created by Tolkien, has grown into a global phenomenon. Spanning films, games, merchandise, tourism and countless licensed products, this makes it one of the most successful examples of creative intellectual property ever created.
But let's start at the beginning...

In 1937, J.R.R. Tolkien introduced readers to Bilbo Baggins, a comfort-loving hobbit whose quiet existence is interrupted by an unexpected visit from the wizard Gandalf. Before long, Bilbo finds himself swept into an epic adventure, travelling far beyond the Shire on a journey of a lifetime.
The Hobbit may have started as a story told to Tolkien's children, but like many original creative works, it also concerns intellectual property.

Copyright protects original literary works, including books, stories, poems and illustrations . In Tolkien's case, that protection has helped preserve the unique world of Middle-earth and enabled rights holders to license and commercialise it in a variety of ways over the years.

Copyright helps ensure that creators and rights holders can benefit from the value of their work. In Tolkien's case, a story first published in 1937 has continued to generate cultural and commercial value for decades, long after Bilbo first stepped outside his front door. Tolkien died in 1973, so copyright in his works lasts until 2043, 70 years after his death.
An unexpected IP journey
Copyright may have helped protect Tolkien's original stories and characters, but it has also helped Middle-earth travel far beyond the pages of a book.

Through licensing agreements, Tolkien's world has been adapted into films, video games, music, merchandise and tourism experiences enjoyed by fans across the globe. If you’ve sipped a robust black tea from a Hobbit mug or wiped your feet on a Lord of the Rings door mat after an eventful morning hob knobbing around the shire, you’ve experienced the impact of licensing in action.
Nearly a century after it was first published, appreciation for The Hobbit shows no sign of relenting, proving that a great idea can travel far when protected through intellectual property.
Not bad for a Hobbit who never wanted an adventure in the first place.
